terms.definition: Rules that decide who can see or do what on a system, and the mechanisms that enforce them.
Software that bombards you with ads, often bundled with free downloads. Some of it also tracks you.
Advanced Encryption Standard. The symmetric cipher used almost everywhere, from Wi-Fi to disk encryption.
Physically isolating a system from other networks, including the internet, so it can’t be reached remotely.
Spotting behaviour that differs from what’s normal, such as a login at 3am from a new country.
Software that detects and removes known malware, traditionally by matching signatures.
Application Programming Interface. A defined way for programs to talk to each other. Exposed APIs are a common attack target.
Advanced Persistent Threat. A skilled, well-resourced attacker, often state-backed, that breaks in quietly and stays hidden for a long time to steal data or spy.
A trace left on a system by activity, such as a log entry, a Prefetch file or a registry key, that investigators use as evidence.
Encryption with a pair of keys: a public key anyone can use to encrypt, and a private key only the owner uses to decrypt.
Every point where an attacker could try to get in: exposed services, apps, accounts, devices and people.
The route an attacker uses to get in, such as a phishing email, an exposed service or a stolen password.
Proving you are who you say you are, for example with a password, a security key or a fingerprint.
Deciding what an authenticated user is allowed to do. Logging in is authentication; opening a file is authorisation.
A hidden way into a system that bypasses normal authentication, often left behind by malware so the attacker can return.
A record of what normal looks like for a system or network, so unusual activity stands out.
Malware regularly calling home to its command-and-control server. The steady rhythm is often how it gets caught.
The defenders. They monitor, detect and respond to attacks and harden systems against them.
A network of infected devices controlled by one attacker, used for spam, credential stuffing or DDoS attacks.
Guessing a password or key by trying huge numbers of combinations until one works.
Writing more data into a memory buffer than it can hold, spilling into neighbouring memory. Attackers use it to hijack a program.
A programme that pays independent researchers for responsibly reporting security flaws.
A scam where attackers impersonate an executive or supplier by email to trick staff into paying invoices or sending data.
The infrastructure attackers use to send instructions to compromised machines and receive stolen data.
A trusted organisation that issues digital certificates, vouching that a public key belongs to a particular website or person.
A documented record of who handled evidence, when and how, so it holds up in an investigation or court.
Confidentiality, Integrity and Availability: the three goals almost every security control serves.
Tools that continuously check cloud accounts for misconfigurations like public storage buckets or over-permissive roles.
Trying usernames and passwords leaked from one site on many others, betting that people reuse passwords.
Tricking a logged-in user’s browser into sending an unwanted request, such as changing their email address.
A security competition or practice challenge where you solve puzzles or hack deliberately vulnerable systems to find hidden ‘flags’.
Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures. A public ID (like CVE-2021-44228) given to a known security flaw so everyone can refer to it.
Common Vulnerability Scoring System. A 0 to 10 score describing how severe a vulnerability is.
A model that breaks an attack into stages, from reconnaissance to actions on objectives, so defenders can disrupt each one.
Parts of the internet reachable only through tools like Tor. Home to criminal marketplaces, leak sites and forums.
An incident where sensitive data is accessed or stolen by someone who shouldn’t have it.
Moving stolen data out of a network to somewhere the attacker controls.
Distributed Denial of Service. Flooding a service with traffic from many machines so real users can’t reach it.
Layering several independent controls so that if one fails, others still stand in the attacker’s way.
Digital Forensics and Incident Response. Investigating what happened in a breach and containing it.
A cryptographic stamp proving who created a file or message and that it hasn’t been changed since.
A bit-for-bit copy of a storage device, made so investigators can examine it without touching the original.
Tools and rules that stop sensitive data from leaving an organisation by email, upload or USB.
A separate network zone for public-facing servers, so a compromise there doesn’t expose the internal network.
Domain Name System. The internet’s phone book, translating names like example.com into IP addresses.
Hiding data or commands inside DNS queries to sneak them past firewalls.
Malware that installs itself just from visiting a compromised or malicious web page.
Studying malware by running it in a safe, isolated environment and watching what it does.
Endpoint Detection and Response. Software on laptops and servers that records activity, detects threats and lets responders isolate machines.
Scrambling data so only someone with the right key can read it.
Any device that connects to a network: laptops, phones, servers, even printers.
A system’s record of what happened, such as logins, process starts and errors. On Windows, each event has an ID like 4624.
Code or a technique that takes advantage of a vulnerability to make a system do something it shouldn’t.
A real attack that security tools failed to flag. Far more dangerous than a false positive.
An alert that looks like an attack but turns out to be harmless. Weeding these out is a big part of a SOC analyst’s day.
Malware that runs in memory or through built-in tools like PowerShell, leaving little or nothing on disk.
A control that allows or blocks network traffic based on rules.
A verified, hashed copy of a disk or memory, taken so analysis never alters the original evidence.
The EU’s General Data Protection Regulation, which sets rules for handling personal data and reporting breaches.
Reducing a system’s attack surface by removing unused services, tightening settings and applying patches.
A fixed-length fingerprint of a file or text (like SHA-256). Analysts use hashes to identify known malware.
A decoy system set up to attract attackers so defenders can study them or detect them early.
HTTP over TLS. The padlock in your browser: traffic between you and the site is encrypted and the site’s identity is checked.
Identity and Access Management. The policies and tools that control who has access to what.
Intrusion Detection System / Intrusion Prevention System. Watches traffic for attacks; an IPS can also block them.
The organised way a team prepares for, detects, contains, removes and recovers from a security incident.
Malware that grabs saved passwords, cookies and crypto wallets from a machine and sends them to the attacker.
Risk from people inside an organisation, whether malicious, careless or tricked.
Evidence that a system may have been breached, such as a malicious IP address, domain or file hash.
A number that identifies a device on a network, like 192.168.1.10 (IPv4) or 2001:db8::1 (IPv6).
Bypassing the restrictions on a device or an AI model to make it do things its makers blocked.
Software or hardware that records every key you press, used to steal passwords and messages.
When an attacker who has broken into one machine moves on to others inside the same network.
Giving each user and program only the access it truly needs, so a compromise does as little damage as possible.
Living-off-the-land binaries. Legitimate built-in tools (like certutil or PowerShell) that attackers abuse to avoid detection.
A hardware identifier burned into a network card, used to deliver traffic on a local network.
Any software designed to harm, spy on or take control of a system: viruses, worms, trojans, ransomware and more.
Analysing a capture of a computer’s RAM to find running processes, network connections and malware that never touched the disk.
Multi-factor authentication. Proving who you are with more than one thing, such as a password plus a code from your phone.
Spamming someone with login approval prompts until they tap ‘approve’ just to make them stop.
A free, public knowledge base of real-world attacker tactics and techniques, used by defenders to describe and detect attacks.
An attacker secretly sitting between two parties, reading or changing what they send each other.
Mean time to detect and mean time to respond. How quickly a security team notices and deals with incidents.
Network Address Translation. Lets many devices share one public IP address, as your home router does.
Open-Source Intelligence. Intelligence gathered from publicly available information like websites, social media and public records.
A regularly updated list of the most critical web application security risks.
A small chunk of data sent across a network, with headers saying where it came from and where it’s going.
A recording of network traffic, usually opened in Wireshark to see exactly what was sent.
A phishing-resistant replacement for passwords that uses a key pair stored on your device.
An app that generates and stores a unique, strong password for every site, so you only remember one.
Trying a few common passwords against many accounts, staying under lockout limits.
An update that fixes a bug or security vulnerability.
The part of an attack that does the damage, such as the ransomware an exploit delivers.
An authorised, simulated attack on a system to find weaknesses before real attackers do.
Techniques attackers use to survive reboots and keep access, like scheduled tasks or registry run keys.
Tricking people into clicking a link, opening a file or handing over credentials, usually by email or message.
Public Key Infrastructure. The certificates, authorities and rules that let us trust public keys at scale.
A step-by-step guide for handling a specific type of alert or incident, so responses are fast and consistent.
A numbered endpoint on a device for a particular service, such as 443 for HTTPS or 22 for SSH.
Probing a host to see which ports are open and what’s listening. Nmap is the classic tool.
Windows files that record which programs ran and when. A goldmine for forensic investigators.
Gaining higher permissions than you started with, for example going from a normal user to administrator or root.
Hiding instructions in content an AI system reads, to make it ignore its rules or leak data.
A server that forwards traffic on your behalf, used for filtering, caching, privacy or intercepting web requests in testing.
Red and blue teams working together, testing attacks and tuning detections side by side.
Malware that encrypts files and demands payment for the key, often while also threatening to leak stolen data.
Malware that gives an attacker full remote control of a machine, usually without the owner noticing.
Remote Desktop Protocol. Windows remote access that, left exposed to the internet, is a favourite ransomware entry point.
The information-gathering phase of an attack: finding people, systems and weaknesses to target.
Attackers working for the organisation. They emulate real adversaries to test how well defences hold up.
Reporting a vulnerability privately to the vendor and giving them time to fix it before going public.
Taking compiled software apart to understand how it works, often to analyse malware.
A connection from a compromised machine back to the attacker, giving them a command line that slips past inbound firewall rules.
The chance that a threat exploits a vulnerability, multiplied by how bad the result would be.
Malware that hides deep in the operating system to conceal itself and other malicious activity.
Random data added to a password before hashing, so identical passwords produce different hashes and precomputed tables don’t work.
An isolated environment where suspicious files can be run safely without affecting real systems.
Teaching staff to recognise phishing, handle data safely and report anything suspicious.
Splitting a network into zones so an attacker who gets into one can’t easily reach the rest.
Stealing a logged-in user’s session token so you can act as them without needing their password.
Apps and devices staff use without the IT or security team’s knowledge or approval.
Security Information and Event Management. A platform that collects logs from across an organisation and raises alerts on suspicious patterns.
A known pattern, like a hash or byte sequence, that security tools match to recognise a specific threat.
Phishing by SMS text message, often posing as a delivery company or bank.
Security Orchestration, Automation and Response. Tools that automate repetitive SOC tasks like enriching alerts or blocking IPs.
Security Operations Centre. The team that monitors an organisation around the clock and responds to security alerts.
Manipulating people, rather than machines, into breaking security rules or giving away information.
Phishing aimed at a specific person, using details about them to make the message convincing.
Faking the source of something, such as an email sender, caller ID or IP address, to appear trustworthy.
Malware that secretly watches what you do and sends it to someone else.
A web attack where malicious input tricks an application into running unintended database commands.
Secure Shell. An encrypted way to log in to and run commands on a remote machine.
Examining a file without running it: its strings, hashes, structure and code.
Compromising a trusted supplier, such as a software update or library, to reach all of its customers at once.
Encryption where the same key locks and unlocks the data. Fast, but both sides need to share the key safely.
A discussion-based rehearsal where a team walks through how they would handle an imagined incident.
The two main transport protocols. TCP guarantees delivery and order; UDP is faster but makes no promises.
The person or group behind an attack, from lone criminals to nation-state teams.
Proactively searching for attackers who have slipped past automated detection.
Information about attackers, their tools and their targets that helps defenders prioritise and detect threats.
A structured look at what you’re protecting, from whom, and how they might attack it.
Putting every recovered event in time order to reconstruct exactly what happened during an incident.
Transport Layer Security. The protocol that encrypts web traffic, email and much more in transit.
A network that routes traffic through several volunteer relays to hide where it came from.
Tactics, techniques and procedures. How a particular attacker tends to operate, which is harder to change than an IP address.
Malware disguised as legitimate software to trick people into running it.
Quickly deciding whether an alert is real, how serious it is and who should handle it.
Registering look-alike domains or package names (like g00gle.com) to catch people’s typos.
Voice phishing: scam phone calls that pose as banks, support desks or colleagues.
Virtual Private Network. An encrypted tunnel between your device and another network.
A weakness in software, hardware or a process that an attacker could exploit.
An automated check of systems against a database of known vulnerabilities and misconfigurations.
Web Application Firewall. Filters HTTP traffic to block attacks like SQL injection and XSS before they reach an app.
Compromising a website a target group often visits, then infecting them when they drop by.
Spear phishing aimed at senior executives, often to authorise large payments.
Malware built purely to destroy data, sometimes disguised as ransomware.
Malware that spreads from machine to machine on its own, without anyone having to run it.
Extended Detection and Response. EDR’s bigger sibling, correlating data from endpoints, email, network and cloud.
A web attack that injects malicious scripts into pages other users will view.
A rule language for describing and detecting malware by its patterns, used widely by analysts.
A security model that never trusts a request just because it comes from inside the network. Every access is verified.
A vulnerability attackers know about before the vendor has a fix, leaving defenders zero days to prepare.
